To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) antigen-primed helper T cells are genetically programmed to recognize antigen in association only with parental H-2 genes, 2) antigen-priming of helper T cells results in the expression of a new surface molecule, the Ia antigen, and 3) the Ia antigen is required for helper T-cell function in the in vivo and in vitro antibody responses

antigen-primed T cells bind selectively to antigen-pulsedd macrophages (Mphi) and that the genetic control of helper T-cell function in the in vitro TNP-antigen response is governed by H-2-linked genes.

antigen-specific murine T cells can be enriched for helper activity by selective binding to Mphi pulsed with the relevant antigen, and that helper T cells are genetically restricted in their ability to collaborate with B lymphocytes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the genetic control of the helper T-cell function in the mouse.
the genetic control of helper T-cell function and with the mechanisms involved in antigen recognition.
the role of H- 2 linked genes in the regulation of helper T-cell function in the murine TNP-SR BC system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the H-2 linked gene(s) controlling helper T-cell function is expressed at the cell surface of both the Mphi and T cell and that it is involved in the antigen-specific recognition of both Mphi and B cell.
H-2-linked genes are required for both the recognition and the expression of T cell help.

the H-2 complex contains a minimum of two separate sets of genes, one of which controls the ability of T cells to recognize antigen in association either with parental H-2d or H-2b gene products and the other of which controls the recognition of the same parental products by B cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
H-2-linked genes control the recognition of helper cells by both Mphi and B cell.
the H-2-linked genes controlling helper T cell function are expressed in two separate populations of helper T-cells.
H-2 linked Ir genes control the recognition of antigen by T helper cells in the context of a particular set of parental H -2 gene products.
The main takeaway from our work is that
T cells can recognize antigen in association not only with self-MHC but also with MHC from the other parent.
the helper T cells in an F1 animal can be divided into two distinct populations, each recognizing antigen in association with one of the parental haplotype products.
the H2 restriction in the helper T cell response is a result of the recognition of the H2 haplotype on the macrophage.
